sumber: KSSM Form 5 Science DSKP (KPM), English for the Dual Language Programme. Written for the app.

t: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, algae.

nota.t: Microorganisms are tiny living things seen only under a microscope: bacteria (prokaryotic cells), fungi (yeast and moulds), protozoa (Amoeba, Paramecium), algae and viruses (not cells; they reproduce only inside host cells). Their growth depends on nutrients, temperature, pH, moisture and light.

t: Bacterial shapes: coccus (sphere), bacillus (rod), spirillum (spiral)
Most bacteria grow best at about 37 °C
Prepare three sterile agar plates
Expose one to air, touch one with a finger, keep one closed as the control
Incubate at 37 °C for 2–3 days
Compare the number of colonies

nota.t: Useful microorganisms make food (yeast in bread and tapai, Lactobacillus in yoghurt), medicines (penicillin from a fungus, vaccines), help farming (nitrogen-fixing bacteria, compost), treat sewage and are used in biotechnology (insulin from modified bacteria).
Fermentation by yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy

Pathogens spread through air (influenza, tuberculosis), water and food (cholera, typhoid), touch (ringworm) and vectors (Aedes mosquitoes carry dengue, Anopheles carry malaria). Prevention: hygiene, sterilisation, immunisation and destroying vectors. Treatment: antibiotics (bacteria only), antifungals and antivirals.

t: Active immunity: the body makes its own antibodies (vaccine)
Passive immunity: antibodies are given (antiserum)
Antibiotics do not work on viruses; finish the full course

v.c: How diseases spread and are prevented

t: Energy value; food production and processing technology.

nota.t: A balanced diet contains all the food classes in the right amounts. Calorific value is the energy released by 1 g of food: carbohydrate 17 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g, fat 38 kJ/g. Plants need macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) and micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B). The nitrogen cycle returns nitrogen to the soil through fixation, nitrification and decay.
Example: 1 g of nut heats 20 g of water by 30 °C. Energy = 20 × 4.2 × 30 = 2 520 J = 2.52 kJ/g.

Food production technology raises yield and quality: genetic engineering (disease-resistant crops), tissue culture (many identical plantlets quickly), hydroponics and aeroponics (no soil), fertigation, aquaculture, selective breeding, biological pest control and precision farming with drones and sensors.

Food processing preserves food by stopping microorganisms and enzymes: heating (pasteurisation at 63 °C for 30 min or 72 °C for 15 s; UHT at 132 °C), cooling and freezing, drying, salting and pickling, canning, irradiation, vacuum packing and preservatives. Health foods and supplements must be used with care and checked for registration.

t: Product life cycle; pollution; conservation.

nota.t: A product's life cycle covers raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use and disposal. A life-cycle assessment measures the environmental impact of each stage. Sustainable products are designed to be repaired, reused or recycled.

v.c: The life cycle of a product

nota.t: Environmental pollution includes air (vehicle smoke, haze), water (factory waste, sewage, oil spills), soil (pesticides, solid waste), noise, thermal and radioactive pollution. Effects: acid rain, ozone thinning, the greenhouse effect, eutrophication and health problems.

t: Acid rain: SO₂ and NO₂ dissolve in rain
Eutrophication: fertiliser → algal bloom → less oxygen

nota.t: Preservation protects nature from disturbance; conservation uses resources sustainably and restores damaged areas. Measures include laws (Environmental Quality Act 1974), national parks, replanting forests, waste treatment, green technology and environmental education.

t: Rate = change in quantity ÷ time; factors and collision theory.

nota.t: The rate of reaction is the change in the amount of reactant or product per unit time, measured from gas released, mass lost, colour change or precipitate formed. Average rate = total change ÷ time; the instantaneous rate is the gradient of the tangent on the graph.

t: Add marble chips to hydrochloric acid in a conical flask
Collect the gas in an inverted burette or gas syringe
Record the volume every 30 seconds
Plot the graph and find the gradient

nota.t: The rate increases with smaller particle size (bigger surface area), higher concentration, higher temperature, a catalyst and higher pressure (for gases). Collision theory: a reaction happens when particles collide with energy above the activation energy in the right orientation; these factors raise the frequency of effective collisions.

t: Catalysts lower the activation energy
Uses: refrigerators slow decay, pressure cookers cook faster, catalysts in industry
Hydrocarbons, alcohols, fats, palm oil, rubber.

nota.t: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are saturated with single bonds, such as methane and ethane. Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) are unsaturated with a double bond, such as ethene, and decolourise bromine water. Petroleum is separated by fractional distillation.

t: Fractions: petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, bitumen
Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O

nota.t: Alcohols have the hydroxyl group (−OH). Ethanol is made by fermenting glucose with yeast and is used as a fuel, solvent and antiseptic. Fats are esters of fatty acids and glycerol; saturated fats raise blood cholesterol. Palm oil is extracted from the mesocarp by sterilising, stripping, digesting, pressing, clarifying and refining, and is rich in vitamin E.

Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene monomers collected as latex from rubber trees. Latex coagulates when acid is added and is kept liquid with ammonia. Vulcanisation with sulphur forms cross-links, making rubber stronger, more elastic and heat resistant, for tyres, gloves and seals.

t: Acid coagulates latex; ammonia prevents coagulation
Vulcanised rubber: harder, more elastic, resists heat and oxidation
Electrolytic and chemical cells.

nota.t: An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to decompose an electrolyte (a molten or aqueous compound that conducts). The anode is connected to the positive terminal and the cathode to the negative. Cations move to the cathode and anions to the anode. Electrolysis is used for electroplating, purifying copper and extracting aluminium.

t: Fill a beaker with copper(II) sulphate solution
Dip in two carbon electrodes
Connect a battery and ammeter
Observe copper deposited at the cathode and oxygen at the anode

nota.t: A chemical (voltaic) cell turns chemical energy into electrical energy through redox reactions. Two different metals stand in an electrolyte; the more electropositive metal is the negative terminal (zinc in the Daniell cell). Examples: dry cells, alkaline cells, lead-acid accumulators, lithium-ion cells.

t: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v; optical instruments.

nota.t: A convex lens converges light to the principal focus F; a concave lens diverges it. Ray diagrams: a ray parallel to the axis passes through F; a ray through the optical centre goes straight. Lens formula: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v; magnification m = v/u.
Example: f = 10 cm, u = 30 cm. 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 → v = 15 cm; m = 0.5 (real, inverted, diminished).

v.c: Image formed by a convex lens

nota.t: Optical instruments: a camera forms a real, inverted, small image; a projector a real, magnified image; a magnifying glass a virtual, upright, magnified image (object inside f); microscopes and telescopes use two convex lenses. Glasses correct short sight (concave lens) and long sight (convex lens).

t: P = F/A; P = ρgh; Pascal, Archimedes, Bernoulli.

nota.t: Pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A, in pascals. Liquid pressure rises with depth and density: P = hρg. Pascal's principle: pressure on an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally (hydraulic jacks and brakes). Archimedes' principle: buoyant force equals the weight of liquid displaced. Bernoulli's principle: faster-moving fluid has lower pressure (aircraft lift).
Example: small piston 2 cm² with 50 N, large piston 100 cm². F₂ = 50 × 100/2 = 2 500 N.

v.c: Pascal's principle in a hydraulic jack

t: Satellites and GPS.

nota.t: Satellites orbit a planet. Artificial satellites are used for communication, weather, remote sensing, navigation and research. Geostationary satellites (about 36 000 km up) orbit once a day and appear fixed. The GPS uses at least 24 satellites; a receiver times signals from at least four satellites to find its position by trilateration.

t: Satellites send their time and position
The receiver works out distance = speed of light × time
Distances from 3 satellites fix the position
A 4th satellite corrects the clock error
